title: Epidemiology of Gram-Negative Bloodstream Infections in the United States: Results From a Cohort of 24 Hospitals

claims.text: E. coli is the most common Gram-negative organism in bloodstream infections, accounting for 51.0% of isolates.
claims.byte_quote: Escherichia coli (2471, 51.0%) was the most common Gram-negative organism recovered

claims.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae is the second most common Gram-negative bloodstream isolate at 17.3%.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the third most common Gram-negative bloodstream isolate at 8.7%.
ESBL production occurred in 15.7% of eligible isolates.
Western sites had the highest percentage of ESBL producers among eligible isolates (16%).
claims.byte_quote: Western sites had the highest percentage of ESBL producers of total eligible isolates (16%)

claims.text: The median patient age in the Gram-negative bacteremia cohort was 67 years (IQR 55-77).
Patients aged 70 years or older comprised 42.73% of the cohort.
Moderate to severe immunocompromise was present in 34.52% of patients.
32.34% of bacteremia patients were in the intensive care unit.
ESBL-producing organisms were significantly more frequent in White than non-White patients (14.6% vs 9.5%, P<0.01).
claims.byte_quote: there was a statistically significant difference in the percentage of ESBL-producing organisms in White vs non-White patients (14.6 % and 9.5 %, respectively, P<0.01)

claims.text: The urinary tract was the most common source of Gram-negative bacteremia (47.9%).
claims.byte_quote: Most common source of infection was the urinary tract (47.9%)

claims.text: Common sources of Gram-negative bacteremia were urinary tract (47.9%), intra-abdominal (14.5%), and hepatobiliary (11.4%).
claims.byte_quote: Common sources of infection included urinary tract (47.9%), intra-abdominal (14.5%), and hepatobiliary (11.4%)

claims.text: Respiratory tract sources accounted for 5.60% of Gram-negative bacteremias.
